titleStmt.title: Improved Results for Guaranteeing Safety Despite Physical Errors in CPS's

analytic.title: Improved Results for Guaranteeing Safety Despite Physical Errors in CPS's

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: A recent paper declares a 'physical error' to have occurred in an autonomous mobile CPS if it fails to pinpoint its location to within an acceptable degree of accuracy, and proposes an innovative approach for dealing with such physical errors without compromising safety properties. We further generalize the proposed approach to enhance its applicability to a wider range of conditions than is currently possible. We also show that some schedulability analysis that was derived in this recent paper for this approach is too optimistic, and present a fix to get rid of unwarranted optimism.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The process by which an autonomous mobile CPS such as a self-driving car determines its precise physical position (upon, e.g., an internally stored map) is referred to as 'localization.' A paper [1] that was presented at RTAS earlier this year, titled Guaranteeing Safety Despite Physical Errors in Cyber-Physical Systems, defined a 'physical error' by such a CPS to be a failure to localize with an acceptable degree of accuracy. It proposed an innovative workload model for representing the computations that implement localization in popular selfdriving software frameworks such as Autoware [2], [3], and devised mechanisms for ensuring safety despite the occurrence of physical errors. In this paper, we (i) show that some schedulability analysis in [1] is too optimistic and may cause deadline misses, and correct this analysis; and (ii) generalize the workload model of [1] in two directions that increase its expressiveness in semantically meaningful ways.

The problem considered in [1]. In the workload model that was proposed in [1] (we will describe this model in greater detail in Section II), a subset of the computations that are performed by Autoware is represented as the directed acyclic graph (DAG) shown in Figure 1(a) -here the vertex v 2 represents the localization operation. Each vertex v i is characterized by a worst-case execution time c(v i ). This DAG is invoked repeatedly to execute upon a dedicated bank of m ≥ 1 identical processors. Each invocation is required to complete execution within a specified duration D, and successive invocations occur at least D time units apart The first two authors were supported in part by IITP grants funded by the Korean government (MSIT) (No.2015-0-00209, SW Starlab and No.2021-0-02068, AI Innovation Hub) and also in part by AI Institute at Seoul National University (AIIS). The third author received support from the National Science Foundation (NSF CPS-1932530 and CNS-2141256). (hence each invocation completes before the next is released -from an analysis perspective, this simplifies the problem to that of analyzing just a single invocation). On any given invocation, if the localization operation represented as vertex v 2 is successful in pinpointing physical location to within a specified acceptable error threshold, then all the vertices in the DAG of Figure 1(a) are executed. However if vertex v 2 fails to determine physical location to within the specified acceptable error threshold despite having executed for a duration c(v 2 ), it flags a physical error. Upon this happening, the vertices {v 4 , v 5 , v 6 } are not executed for this invocation ( [1] refers to these as a dangling subgraph -see Section II); instead, a separate back-up vertex v b is executed 1 that computes the input needed by vertex v 7 . (The DAG that gets executed in the case that a physical error occurs is depicted in its entirety in Figure 1(b).) In this manner safety is maintained, but at a performance price -the vehicle does not perform as one would have ideally liked (i.e., if vertices v 4 -v 6 , tasked with "mak[ing] the car follow the optimal path from the cars current position to the final destination" [1] had also executed).

In order to minimize the likelihood of a physical error, we should maximize the duration for which the vertex v 2 is allowed to execute. (In the terminology of [1], a vertex like this for which WCET should be maximized is called a selflooping node -see Section II-for reasons that are explained in [1].) This translates to the following optimization problem, solving which is the main focus of [1]: maximize the value assigned to the WCET of the self-looping node, such that each invocation of the DAG completes within an interval of duration D, regardless of whether it flags a physical error or not during the invocation. This work. It is evident that (correct and) efficient solutions to the optimization problem above enhances the effectiveness of the framework in [1]. In this work we take a close look at this optimization problem, and make the following contributions.

We show that one of the two algorithms that were proposed in [1] for solving this optimization problem is too optimistic in the sense that it may assign a larger WCET value to the self-looping node than is safe; this invalidates the associated safety claim and could potentially result in missed deadlines. We propose a simple fix that corrects the algorithm in [1]. 2) Separately, we develop a different algorithm for solving this optimization problem. We will show that this algorithm can be extended to solve a generalization to the problem that was solved in [1]; so far as we can tell, the algorithm in [1] is not extendible in this manner.

3) The workload model used in [1] requires that all the vertices of the dangling subgraph are (immediate or transitive) successors of the self-looping node. We argue that getting rid of this restriction is semantically meaningful, and explain how to do so. 4) Allowing for the presence of multiple self-looping nodes in a single DAG was listed in [1] as an important practicallymotivated extension to their proposed model. We study this problem in detail: we identify some ambiguities that must be resolved in defining this issue formally, suggest a resolution to these ambiguities, and obtain an efficient algorithm for solving the resulting problem.

Organization. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Since our work builds upon the innovations introduced in [1], we briefly review both the workload model and some of the results presented there in Section II. In Section III we formally define (Definition 1) a specific problem whose solution is central to the approach advocated in [1], show that an algorithm that was proposed in [1] for solving this problem may be too optimistic, and propose a simple modification that removes unwarranted optimism. In Section IV we present an alternative algorithm that also (correctly) solves the problem of Definition 1. In Section V we remove the restriction that all vertices of the dangling subgraph be successors of the self-looping node. In Section VI we formally define, and propose an efficient algorithm for solving, the generalization to multiple self-looping nodes of the problem considered in [1].
We have conducted simulation experiments similar to the ones reported in [1] for evaluating the effectiveness of our proposed algorithms; we report on our findings in Section VII.

div.head: II. OVERVIEW OF PRIOR WORK [1]
div.p: The relevance to CPS of the workload model proposed in [1] was forcefully and convincingly argued there, by emphasizing a range of relevant scenarios that are accurately modeled by it. Here we briefly review this proposed model, and provide a high-level description of the approach taken in [1] for scheduling and schedulability analysis of workloads so represented.
Workload model. An instance is represented by a tuple
div.formula: G, v s , V dangle , v b , m, D(1)
div.p: where
div.formula: • G = (V, E, c) is a DAG with vertices V , each v ∈ V denoting a job; edges E ⊆ V × V denoting precedence
div.p: constraints between pairs of jobs; and worst-case execution time (WCET) function c :
div.formula: V → N with c(v i ) denoting the WCET of the job v i ∈ V . • v s ∈ V is called the self-looping node. • V dangle ⊂ (V \ {v s }) is called the dangling subgraph. Each
div.p: vertex in V dangle is additionally required to be an immediate or transitive successor vertex of v s -in Section V we will discuss why it is desirable to get rid of this requirement, and how to do so.
div.formula: • v b is another job (not in V ), called the backup node, with a specified WCET c(v b ).
div.p: • This instance is to be executed upon a dedicated platform of m processors to complete within an interval of duration no larger than D (i.e., each invocation of the instance has a deadline that is D time units after its invocation).

The semantics of execution of the instance represented by Expression 1 is as follows. The DAG is invoked repeatedly, with successive invocations separated by a duration ≥ D time units; each invocation is required to complete execution within D time units. On each invocation, the job represented by the self-looping node v s either (i) completes upon having executed for no more than c(v s ) time units; or (ii) executes for c(v s ) time units and then flags a physical error. If v s completes upon having executed for no more than c(v s ) time units, then the remainder of the DAG must complete execution. If, however, v s declares a physical error, then the vertices in the dangling subgraph V dangle do not need to execute during this invocation; instead, the backup node v b must execute. All incoming edges to vertices in V dangle become predecessor vertices to v b , which in turn becomes the predecessor vertex to all vertices for which vertices in V dangle are predecessors.

The approach of [1]. As we had stated in Section I, the approach of [1] is based upon maximizing the value of c(v s ), the execution budget (WCET parameter) that can be assigned to the self-looping node v s , such that each invocation of the instance completes within an interval of duration D regardless of whether v s executes successfully or flags a physical error.

To determine this, the approach of [1] computes separately for 1) the specified graph G, and 2) the graph obtained from G by replacing the vertices in V dangle by the back-up node v b (as described above), the largest value that c(v s ) could be assigned while guaranteeing that the graph will compute execution within an interval of duration D. Upon computing both these values, the approach of [1] simply assigns c(v s ) the smaller of the two values so computed. 2 Example 1. Consider again the example from Section I, the two graphs for which are depicted in Figure 1. Let us suppose that c(v i ) = 1 for each of the vertices {v 1 , v 3 -v 7 }, while the backup node v b has WCET c(v b ) = 3. Suppose that D = 7, and there are arbitrarily many processors available. It is evident that the DAG of Figure 1(a) will complete within the deadline for values of c(v 2 ) ≤ 3; however, the DAG of Figure 1(b) will complete within the deadline only for values of c(v 2 ) ≤ 2. Therefore, for this example [1] would assign c(v 2 ) the value min(3, 2) = 2.

In this manner, [1] reduces the problem of optimizing the budget assigned to the self-looping node v s to the problem of determining the largest value we can assign to the WCET parameter of a single node in a given "regular" DAG task. Two approaches were investigated in [1] for solving this problem. One, called Classic Bound Based Analysis [1, Sec. V], is based upon the classical List Scheduling algorithm (LS) [4], [5], for which quantitative bounds on performance are known. The other is based on the Concurrent Producer/ Consumer (CPC) heuristic [6]; while this heuristic has been shown in [6] to perform well upon randomly-generated synthetic workloads, there are no quantitative bounds on its performance. In the remainder of this paper we restrict attention to Classic Bound Based Analysis. One consequence of this is that we may consider either non-preemptive or preemptive scheduling (unlike [1], which restricts attention to non-preemptive scheduling). This is desirable: there is nothing in Autoware per se that forbids preemption -we have been informed 3 by the authors of [1] that their sole reason for requiring non-preemptive scheduling is that CPC does not allow preemptions.

Related work. Our work primarily extends the recently reported work of Han et al. [1], and is therefore very closely related to [1]; please see [1, Sec. II] for a discussion of the work that they build off. Briefly, they cite three fields of related work: those dealing with real-time DAG scheduling such as [5], [6] (although they point out that none of the works they cite consider non-fixed WCETs), imprecise computation [7], [8], and Sha's Simplex architecture [9]; they point out significant differences between their model and the imprecise computation/ simplex models. 2 We point out here that considering the two DAGs separately and assigning c(vs) the smaller value is correct only because of the constraint in the model of [1] that all of V dangle are successors of vs. In Section V, we will consider what happens when we remove this constraint. 3 Personal communication.

div.head: III. THE MAX-WCET PROBLEM
div.p: As we saw in Section II above, the approach in [1] to determining the largest WCET value that may safely be assigned to the self-looping node is by reducing it to the problem of computing the largest WCET value that may safely be assigned to a node in a "regular" graph. So, consider a DAG G = (V, E, c) where V denotes the set of jobs, E ⊆ V × V the precedence constraints between pairs of jobs, and c : V → N the worst-case execution durations (WCETs) of the jobs, that is to be scheduled upon m dedicated processors to complete within an interval of duration D. In the Classic Bound Based Analysis [1], the DAG is assumed to be scheduled during run-time Graham's List Scheduling algorithm (LS) [4], [5]. In LS the jobs are prioritized in some fixed order prior to runtime. During runtime at each instant the highest-priority eligible jobs are executed upon the available processors (with a job being eligible if all its predecessor jobs have completed execution). LS is defined in both preemptive and non-preemptive forms: for preemptive LS a job will preempt a currently executing lower-priority job upon becoming eligible, while such preemption is forbidden for non-preemptive LS.

A critical path in a DAG is defined to be a sequence of precedence-constrained vertices in the DAG for which the sum of the WCET's is the largest from amongst all sequences of precedence-constrained vertices. It has been shown [4], [5] that for any priority ordering of the vertices, both preemptive and non-preemptive LS will schedule any DAG G = (V, E, c) upon m unit-speed processors, with a makespan not exceeding
div.formula: W G m + L G × 1 - 1 m (2)
div.p: where W G denotes the cumulative WCET of all the vertices in V and L G , the cumulative WCET of a critical path G (W G is commonly referred to as the 'work,' and L G the 'span,' of the DAG G). Since WG m and L G are both obvious lower bounds on the makespan of any schedule for this DAG upon m processors, it immediately follows that LS schedules any DAG with a makespan that is no larger than 2 -1 m times the optimal makespan.
We can now formally specify the problem that lies at the heart of the Classic Bound Based Analysis [1]:

The reason for, and implications of, the unwarranted optimism. Without going into too much detail, we can briefly identify the heart of the problem with the algorithm of [1, Sec.V] as this: it implicitly assumes that the self-looping node (i.e., vertex whose WCET is to be maximized) lies on a critical path once its WCET has been increased. As the example above shows, that is not necessarily true. We emphasize that overallocating execution budget to the self-looping node (as in the example above), invalidates the guarantee that the DAG will always complete execution within an interval of duration D -if the deadline is safety-critical then assigning budgets according to the algorithm of [1, Sec.V] constitutes a potential safety hazard. We have performed some simulation experiments upon synthetically-generated workloads (discussed in Section VII); a sampling of the results is depicted in Figure 3. The derived parameter density is defined [1] as the work (sum of WCETs) of the DAG, normalized by the available computation capacity upon which to execute it: as can be seen from Figure 3, budget overallocation tends to be a factor of concern upon heavily-loaded platforms.

A simple fix. We saw above that [1] erred in assuming that the self-looping node always lies on a critical path after its WCET has been increased. We will therefore also consider the other possibility -that it does not lie on a critical path even after its WCET is increased-and compute the largest WCET it could have if this were to be the case. We then simply assign the self-looping node a WCET equal to the smaller of the two values so computed.

We point out first that for the latter scenario (i.e., the selflooping node v s not lying on a critical path after its WCET is increased) to happen, it must be the case that v s is initially 4 We have confirmed this fact from the authors of [1]. not already on a critical path. In Section IV below we will see (Expression 6) how to efficiently determine the maximum cumulative WCET of any precedence-constrained sequence of vertices that includes a given vertex. Here we first use this to check that v s is not on a critical path (prior to increasing its WCET), by verifying that the maximum cumulative WCET of any precedence-constrained sequence of vertices that includes vertex v s is strictly smaller than the critical length of the entire DAG. If this is the case, let W denote the cumulative WCET of all the remaining vertices (i.e., all vertices in (V \ {v s })) and L the critical path length. In order to guarantee that the bound of Expression 2 does not exceed D, we need

Example 3. For the instance of Figure 2 that was discussed in Example 2 above, Expression 3 assigns c(v 1 ) a value of 9; since min(13, 9) = 9, this is the value that should be assigned to c(v 1 ). It may be verified that for the resulting DAG, Expression 2 evaluates to 20 which equals the specified deadline; thus, 9 is the largest value c(v 1 ) may take and still satisfy Expression 2.

div.head: V. MODEL EXTENSION: A MORE GENERAL DANGLING SUBGRAPH
div.p: The workload model of [1] (that we described in Section II above) imposes the restriction that all vertices in the dangling subgraph V dangle be (immediate or transitive) successor vertices of the self-looping node v s . We believe it is semantically meaningful to weaken this restriction if possible; e.g., in the motivating Autoware use-case scenarios used in [1] it is reasonable to decide to not execute jobs responsible for vehicle comfort and entertainment features (that are not locationdependent and thus not successor jobs of the localization job) in the event of the self-looping node flagging a physical error.

The workload model of [1] assumes that individual nodes are executed non-preemptively; however, (as we had pointed out towards the end of Section II), this is solely due to the fact that the CPC heuristic [6] used in [1] is not defined for preemptive scheduling. On the other hand Classic Bound Based Analysis [1, Sec. V], which uses List Scheduling, is defined for preemptive as well as non-preemptive scheduling. In this work we are restricting our attention to Classic Bound Based Analysis [1, Sec. V], and so may choose to allow for preemption. And when preemptive scheduling is used, it becomes feasible to permit V dangle to contain vertices that are not successor vertices of v s ; consider the following example.

Example 5. The DAG in Figure 5 (a) is to be scheduled upon m = 3 processors to complete within a specified deadline D. div.p: Without preemption, however, job v 4 , which is in V dangle and therefore does not need to complete when a physical error happens, cannot be removed and replaced by v b ; therefore, v b will only begin execution at time D and complete at time 2D -1, and so the instance would miss its deadline.

The critical observation here is that in preemptive List Scheduling, a job will preempt a currently executing lowerpriority job upon becoming eligible 7 to execute. Hence the priority ordering used for List Scheduling should prioritize jobs not in V dangle above those that are in V dangle . If this is done, it is straightforward to observe that jobs in V dangle would only be executing prior to v s completing execution if there were no other jobs awaiting execution (i.e., the processors would otherwise have been idling), and therefore the instance will execute correctly to complete by its deadline even in those invocations where the self-looping node flags a physical error.

div.head: VI. MODEL EXTENSION: MULTIPLE SELF-LOOPING NODES
div.p: Obtaining a generalization of the workload model in [1] that allows for multiple vertices to be designated as self-looping nodes was identified as an important practically relevant direction for extending the applicability of their ideas. Although some heuristic approaches were proposed for doing so, a formal model for multiple self-looping nodes was not defined in [1]; instead, this feature (of multiple self-looping nodes) was presented via a somewhat simple illustrative example. In Section VI-A below we examine a different example that brings to light some ambiguities that must be resolved in order to formulate the multiple self-looping nodes problem formally. In Section VI-B we suggest one reasonable resolution to these ambiguities, and propose a formal model accordingly. In Section VI-C we extend the classical analysis to the multiple self-looping node problem as defined by our proposed formal model.

div.head: A. AN ILLUSTRATIVE EXAMPLE
div.p: If multiple self-looping nodes are specified in a single DAG, then for each we need to also specify a corresponding dangling subgraph 8 (of nodes that do not need to execute upon it flagging a physical error) and a corresponding backup node (that does). Suppose that vertices v 2 , v 4 , and v 5 in Figure 1 (reproduced in Figure 6, bottom right) were all designated to be self-looping nodes, with the following corresponding dangling subgraphs and backup nodes: self-looping node dangling subgraph back-up node

Upon any invocation of this problem instance, different combinations of the self-looping nodes may flag physical errors; hence, several different 'failure' scenarios are possible during any given invocation of the instance:
• No physical errors are flagged (see Figure 6 (a)).

• Node v 2 flags a physical error; consequently the self-looping nodes v 4 and v 5 , both belonging to the dangling subgraph for v 2 , do not execute (see Figure 6 (b)). • One of v 4 or v 5 flags a physical error (see Figures 6 (c)-(d)).

• Nodes v 4 and v 5 both flag physical errors. This last failure scenario presents a dilemma. As per the single self-looping node semantics from [1] (and described in Section II above), all incoming edges to the dangling subgraph 8 For ease of presentation we will assume these dangling subgraphs satisfy the constraint that we had gotten rid of in Section V, that all vertices in V dangle are successors of vs. Getting rid of this assumption for the multiple self-looping case is straightforward, but the details are somewhat tedious and may obscure the main takeaway message of this section.

for v 4 (the dangling subgraph for v 5 , respectively) should now be incident on the backup node v b,4 (the backup node v b,5 , resp.). But this implies that the edge (v 5 , v 6 ) be redirected to v b,4 , and the edge (v 4 , v 6 ) be redirected to v b,5 . However, v 4 and v 5 have both failed, and hence the outputs that they were expected to generate are instead generated by v b,4 and v b,5 respectively; this implies that the redirected edges form a cycle between the backup vertices v b,4 and v b,5 ! -see Figure 6 (e).

div.head: B. MULTIPLE SELF-LOOPING NODES: A FORMAL MODEL
div.p: We propose a formal model for instances with multiple self-looping nodes that essentially defines away the problem identified in Section VI-A above, by requiring the system developer to explicitly specify the system behavior that is desired in the event of multiple self-looping nodes flagging physical errors during the same invocation. That is, the system developer is required to specify different modes corresponding to combinations of self-looping nodes that may flag physical errors during the same invocation. To do so, the system developer must specify the following. E,c) is a DAG as in [1] (and as described in Section II). • V s ⊂ V is the set of self-looping nodes.

• A number of modes is defined. Each mode is specified as a 3-tuple (S, V dangle,S , v b,S ), where 1) S ⊂ V s is a subset of the set of self-looping nodes; 2) V dangle,S ⊂ (V \ S), with the additional constraint that each vertex in V dangle,S is an immediate or transitive successor to each vertex in S; and 3) v b,S is a different job (i.e., not in V ), with an associated specified WCET c(v b,S ). This mode (S, V dangle,S , v b,S ) is defined to occur in an invocation when all the vertices in S flag physical errors during that invocation. In the event of this mode occurring, none of the vertices in V dangle,S need execute; instead, the single job v b,S executes. All incoming edges to vertices in V dangle,S become incoming edges to v b,S , and all outgoing edges from vertices in V dangle,S become outgoing edges from v b,S . (We point out that the non-occurrence of any physical error during an invocation may also be conveniently represented as a mode (∅, ∅, v dud ) where v dud is a dummy node with WCET c(v dud ) set equal to zero.) Example 6. The motivating example of Section VI-A is conveniently represented using the notation introduced above in this section, with V s , the set of self-looping nodes, equal to {v 2 , v 4 , v 5 }, and five modes: 1) Mode (∅, ∅, v dud ) -this is the mode that is depicted in Figure 6 (a). 2) Mode ({v 2 }, {v 4 , v 5 , v 6 }, v b,2 ) -depicted in Figure 6 for the instance considered in Section VI-A (also see Figure 6).

The last mode above is particularly noteworthy -as we saw earlier (Figure 6 (e)), the behavior of this example system is ambiguously specified when both v 4 and v 5 signal physical errors, without the use of the model we are proposing in this section.

div.head: C. MULTIPLE SELF-LOOPING NODES: COMPUTING WCETS
div.p: In Section III we had discussed (and proposed a fix for) the algorithm in [1] for computing the WCET for the self-looping node when there is only one self-looping node present in a DAG; in Section IV we presented an alternative algorithm, based on the use of linear programming, for doing so. The approach of [1] does not seem to generalize to when multiple self-looping nodes are present in a single DAG. In this section we will represent the problem of determining the WCETs of multiple self-looping nodes in a single DAG as a Linear Program that generalizes the one in Section IV. 9Let us suppose that k distinct modes (including (∅, ∅, v dud ), corresponding to the occurrence of no physical errors) are specified for the instance under consideration. As we saw from our example in Section VI-A (also see Figures 6 and7), the occurrence of each of the k modes may require a different DAG to be executed. We now extend the algorithm presented in Section IV to represent the schedulability conditions for all these DAGs as a single linear program. In this linear program, there will be one variable for each self-looping node, to represent its WCET. Then for each of the k DAGs corresponding to the k modes, we will separately • Have variables to denote its work W and its span L, and for each vertex v in this DAG, its earliest start time est(v) • Write constraints upon these variables, as well as the ("global") variables representing the WCETs of the selflooping nodes, to denote the constraints on earliest start times imposed by the edges in the DAG (analogous to We can similarly count the number of constraints: there is one per source node (for a total of 5 across all the DAGs) plus (8 + 5 + 8 + 8 + 8 =) 37 instantiations of Expression 7 corresponding to the edges plus one per DAG (for a total of 5) instantiation of (Expression 9) for each sink vertex plus 1 per DAG (for a total of 5) instantiation of Expression 8 plus 1 per DAG (for a total of 5) instantiation of Expression 10, for a total of 57 constraints.

It is fairly evident that the LP constructed as described above does indeed represent feasible solutions to the problem of assigning WCET values to the self-looping nodes in order to ensure that the makespan bound of Expression 2 for the DAG corresponding to each mode does not exceed D. It remains to specify an objective function that maximizes the WCET values that are so assigned. This step is necessarily dictated by semantic considerations: what form of optimization does the system designer desire? Generally speaking, a rich set of desiderata are expressible with linear objective functions. For instance setting the objective function to be the sum of the variables representing the WCETs of the self-looping nodes would dimension the system maximally, but may not assign values equitably across the variables. If on the other hand the objective is to maximize the value assigned to each of them, then one would introduce an additional variable B, add one constraint per self-looping node that its WCET be ≥ B, and set maximizing B to be the objective function. (One could similarly express a constraint that the WCET of one selflooping node should be twice as large as that of another by making requiring that one of these variables be ≥ 2B, and so on.)

div.head: VII. EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION
div.p: We now report on our evaluation experiments, upon both synthetically-generated workloads (Section VII-A) and the navigation algorithms found in Autoware [2], [3] modified as shown in Figure 8 (Section VII-B).

div.head: A. UPON SYNTHETIC WORKLOADS
div.p: We used the detailed description provided in [1, Sec. VII-A] to implement the synthetic workload generator that was used in [1]. We also implemented the two baseline algorithms, BASE LARGE and BASE SMALL (BASE LARGE imposes a larger computational load than BASE SMALL), that were used in [1] for the purposes of comparison.

We have already briefly mentioned (see Figure 3) the findings of our experiments demonstrating the optimism that is inadvertently introduced by the original Classic algorithm [1], which showed that this optimism tends to increase with increasing workload. Let us now explain the plot of Figure 3 in a bit more detail. The x-axis is labeled with density, defined (in [1]) as W/(mD) -the sum of the WCETs, normalized by the available computation capacity upon which to execute it. The label on the y-axis denotes the fraction of generated workloads upon which the original Classic algorithm [1] over-allocates budget and may thus cause critical failures, a concept also defined in [1]: in the context of the motivating application of localization, a critical failure occurs when either the localization error falls below a threshold, or the DAG fails to complete by its deadline.

By design, correct implementations of the Classic algorithm (both for single and for multiple self-looping nodes) will never experience critical failures; however BASE SMALL and BASE LARGE may do so since they do not have a safety backup upon which to fall back in the event that their localization operation does not complete on time. In order to estimate the benefits of the fact that our algorithm generalizes the model of [1] by being able to accommodate multiple self-looping nodes, we measured the critical failure ratios of the baseline algorithms in the presence of more than one self-looping node -the findings are plotted in Figure 9. The top left plot reveals that when there is just a single self-looping node (which could be modeled using prior work) then the critical failure ratio is smaller than 30% for BASE SMALL and 10% for BASE LARGE upon our synthetic workloads; however the remaining three graphs in Figure 9 show that both rates exhibit an increasing trend with increasing number of self-looping nodes, exceeding 70% for BASE SMALL and approaching 40% for BASE LARGE in the presence of four self-looping nodes. This adds further credibility to the observation in [1] that extending their model to allow for the representation of multiple self-looping nodes (as we have done) is a practically meaningful generalization.

div.head: B. UPON AUTOWARE
div.p: We have also repeated the implementation experiments upon Autoware [2], [3] that were reported in [1, Section VII-B], but using the corrected (i.e., no longer optimistic) version of the algorithm for solving the MAX-WCET problem (Definition 1). The DAG structure of the original Autoware is shown in Figure 8 (a) -it is not important for our purposes to understand all the functionalities represented by the nodes of the graph (please see [1, Section VII-B] for a detailed explanation). The vertex labeled 'ndt matching' is designated as the self-looping node, and the dangling subgraph (V dangle ) is enclosed within the dotted polygon. The DAG that gets executed in the event of the self-looping node flagging a physical error is depicted in Figure 8 (b) -here the backup node is the one labeled 'LKAS' (which runs the Lane-Keeping Assistance System algorithm [11]).

As in [1], we simulated an autonomous vehicle in real time in the SVL simulated physical environment [12], using the measured node WCETs reported in [1, Table I]. Figure 10 reports on our findings. Figure 10 (a) compares the car's centre offsets for approximately 16 sec driving by the original Autoware (with parameters chosen as reported in [1]), as well as by a modified version that switches to the Figure 8 (b) DAG in the event that the self-looping node flags a physical error. At time approximately 10 sec, the car under the control of the original (unmodified) Autoware begins drifting from the center lane and eventually crosses over the lane boundary soon after (at about 11 sec) -this constitutes a critical failure. This failure comes about due to the 'ndt matching' node in Figure 8 (a) being unable to compute location with acceptable accuracy within its allocated execution budget (its WCET). However when this happens upon our modified implementation of Autoware, a physical error is flagged and the DAG of Occasional large values, e.g., the peak occurring just prior to 8 sec, cause the 'ndt matching' node to eventually completely lose track of the location. However the car under the control of the modified version of Autoware always keeps close to the center of the lane. Also, the measured execution time of 'ndt matching', depicted as the dashed line in Figure 10, is always below the assigned WCET of 61 ms that was determined using the algorithm developed in this paper for solving the MAX-WCET problem. Instead, the safety backup, i.e., LKAS, comes in and just keeps the car along the centre of the lane until the 'ndt matching' rolls back.
Figure 10 shows such safety backup duration of approximately [8.1 sec, 16 sec] marked as the gray area.

div.head: VIII. SUMMARY
div.p: An innovative mechanism was recently proposed [1] for ensuring safety in the presence of run-time uncertainty in safetycritical CPS's. We have generalized the work in [1] in two practically significant directions. One, we remove a restriction in the model of [1] that requires that only successor nodes of the self-looping node may be dropped upon the occurrence of a physical error . Second, we allow for multiple vertices to be designated as self-looping nodes -this provides a feature that was emphasized in [1] as being particularly desirable. We have also identified circumstances in which some schedulability analysis that was developed in [1] is too optimistic, and have provided a fix that prevents such optimism. We have evaluated our proposed algorithms upon both synthetically generated workloads and an Autoware example use-case that was also the one used for evaluation in [1].
